blocks.title: Velocity selector
blocks.text: A velocity selector is a device used to determine the velocity of a charged particle. In it, electric and magnetic forces are applied to the moving particle in such a way that they balance each other only for one value of velocity, allowing the particle to continue moving with a constant velocity.

Consider a particle with a positive charge +q that enters a uniform magnetic field B at a right angle to it with a velocity v. The magnetic force acts on the particle in the upward direction (Fig. 10.11). To balance this magnetic force, an electric force must act downward on the particle.

blocks.alt: A magnetic field points into the page, shown by crosses. A positive charge moves to the right with velocity v and feels a force F = q v B pointing up the page. A box says F = q (v x B) is at right angles to both v and B, so it changes the direction of motion but not the speed.
blocks.caption: Magnetic force on a positive charge moving through a field into the paper (original diagram after Figure 10.11).

blocks.text: A velocity selector consists of a cylindrical tube located within a magnetic field B. Inside the tube is a parallel plate capacitor that creates a uniform electric field E, oriented perpendicular to the magnetic field B (Fig. 10.12). When the charged particle enters the left end of the tube, the magnetic force acts upward while the electric force acts downward, in the direction of E, on the positively charged particle. If the strengths of the electric and magnetic fields are adjusted appropriately, these forces cancel each other out. With no net force acting on the particle, its velocity v remains constant in accordance with Newton's first law; the particle moves in a straight line at constant velocity and exits the right end of the tube. Particles with velocities different from v are deflected and do not exit at the right end.

blocks.alt: A positive charge enters between a positive top plate and a negative bottom plate, in a magnetic field into the page. The electric force qE pushes it down and the magnetic force qvB pushes it up. When qE = qvB, that is v = E / B, the charge goes straight through.
blocks.caption: Velocity selector: a charge between capacitor plates in a magnetic field (original diagram after Figure 10.12).

blocks.text: The magnitude of the velocity selected follows directly. As v is perpendicular to both B and E, the magnetic force (upward) is Bqv and the electric force (downward) is qE. For no deflection of the particle, Bqv = qE, or v = E/B ... (10.15).

blocks.title: Example 10.4
blocks.text: Alpha particles ranging in speed from 1000 m s^-1 to 2000 m s^-1 enter a velocity selector where the electric intensity is 300 V m^-1 and the magnetic induction is 0.20 T. Which particles will move undeviated through the field? Solution: E = 300 V m^-1 = 300 N C^-1, B = 0.20 T. Only those particles pass for which the electric force qE balances the magnetic force Bqv (Fig. 10.12): qE = Bqv, so v = E/B = 300 N C^-1/0.20 N A^-1 m^-1 = 1500 m s^-1. The alpha particles with speed 1500 m s^-1 move undeviated.

blocks.title: Example 10.5
blocks.text: A charged particle moves through a velocity selector at constant velocity in a straight line. The electric field of the selector is 4.8 x 10^3 N C^-1 and the magnetic field is 0.2 T. When the electric field is turned off, the particle travels on a circular path of radius 3.0 cm. Find the charge to mass ratio of the particle. Solution: as the particle moves perpendicular to both E and B, qE = Bqv and v = E/B. With the electric field off, the magnetic force provides the centripetal force: Bqv = mv^2/r, so q/m = v/(Br). Putting v = E/B, q/m = E/(B^2 r) = 4.8 x 10^3 N C^-1/((0.2 T)^2 x 3 x 10^-2 m) = 4 x 10^6 C kg^-1.

A force is exerted on a charged particle moving in a magnetic field. In what direction should it move so that no force is exerted on it? Along the field lines, since then theta = 0 and qvB sin theta = 0 (Point to ponder).
